items.title: Teaching a 7B model new books without forgetting
items.summary: Qwen2.5-7B learned a series of fact books one at a time and kept its general skills.
items.problem: A client needed Qwen2.5-7B to learn a series of fact books in another language, one book at a time, without forgetting earlier books or losing its general skills.
approach: Book-by-book training with a fresh LoRA per book and a KL anchor.
Data pipeline: Q&A and trap-question generation with open teacher models on vLLM, deduplication, and contamination checks against benchmark test sets.
Evaluation with lm-evaluation-harness, custom exams and LLM-as-judge.
items.outcome: The model answers from the books, rejects false-premise questions, and after the first book scored at or above base on IFEval and GSM8K and within 0.7 points on MMLU. In chained runs, book-1 retention held at 0.94–0.99. It was delivered as a frozen, hash-verified package the client re-runs on their own GPUs with their own seeds.

items.title: 15M and 30M QA models that run in the browser
items.summary: Small question-answering models that answer from a page’s passages, or refuse, on devices without WebGPU.
items.problem: I wanted a chat assistant for this site that answers from its own pages without a large download or WebGPU, and refuses when the passages don’t say.
approach: Pretrained two small decoders from scratch on FineWeb-Edu and FineWeb: Tiny 30M (30.5M parameters) and Ant 15M (14.9M, alternating attention and Mamba2 layers).
Fine-tuned both on about 171K evidence-first examples generated with Qwen3-8B: quote the passage first, then answer, or answer “Source: none”.
Exported each as one int8 ONNX file (SmoothQuant) that runs on onnxruntime-web’s WASM backend: 44 MB for Tiny 30M, 21 MB for Ant 15M.
items.outcome: Both models are on Hugging Face. On held-out pages they refuse unanswerable questions well (refusal AUROC 0.99 for Tiny 30M, 0.986 for Ant 15M).
items.reflection: They are experiments, not production assistants: on this site’s own questions Ant 15M answers 9 of 24 correctly and shows a wrong answer about as often, so they are not on the site yet.

items.title: SQL agents for public-markets research
items.summary: LLM systems for equity-market workflows, with guardrails on what the model can query.
items.problem: At a stealth public-markets startup, analysts need to query market and company data in plain language without the model being able to change or leak data.
approach: SQL agents over 14 relational tables, RAG with Pinecone, and ClickHouse for high-volume market and analytics queries.
Security guardrails on the SQL agent: allowlisted schemas and operations, and blocked destructive or out-of-scope statements, so model output cannot freely mutate or exfiltrate data.
ReAct and supervisor multi-agent patterns, an internal Go agent-orchestration library with typed state and durable runs, and a scraping service that ingests market data.
items.outcome: I lead the engineering of these systems, from the agents and guardrails to the orchestration library and the data ingestion behind them.

items.title: Qwen fine-tuning
items.summary: Looking at what changes when I fine-tune a model—and how I check it.
items.problem: I’ve been working with Qwen fine-tuning to explore how a model learns from source material. The question extends beyond training loss: I want to know whether its answers are supported and whether it retains other capabilities.
approach: I’ve worked with LoRA adapters rather than updating every model weight.
I’ve kept source-specific training examples separate from general examples, with answer-token losses and isolated sequence packing.
I’ve used held-out questions and source-based answer reviews alongside training logs. I’ve also explored regularization against the base model’s responses.
items.outcome: I’m comparing training choices with answer reviews on held-out questions. This is an experiment in training and evaluation. The browser playground on this site uses a separate, unmodified pretrained Qwen model.
items.reflection: A lower loss and a better answer are different checks. Source-word overlap can help me inspect an answer, but it cannot establish that the answer addresses the question.

items.title: Experimental Brain
items.summary: Connecting what a model observes with what a small actor does next.
items.problem: I wanted a way to inspect the gap between an observation, an action and a language model’s description of what might happen next.
approach: I connected a V-JEPA 2 encoder to short video samples and recorded the resulting embeddings with their model revision and preprocessing details.
I built a small grid simulation with an explicit rule-based policy. Motion allows a step; a path planner chooses a route around an obstacle.
I kept the optional LLM narration separate from perception and control. I can step through the actor and export a trace of the run.
items.outcome: The site includes real recorded V-JEPA outputs and a separate live-perception service. The browser can replay recordings without downloading the encoder. Live perception requires a configured service; the actor is a demonstration, not a trained robotics policy.
items.reflection: A similarity score is not a confidence estimate, and a plausible narration is not an observation. I make those distinctions visible in the experiment.

items.title: Robot fleet scaling
items.summary: 10× robot fleet capacity on the same hardware.
items.problem: The robot fleet platform ran on a 4-core / 16 GB machine and topped out at 8–10 concurrent robots.
approach: Replaced nested, in-process event handling and Python RQ with a queue-based Celery pipeline: threads for I/O-bound work, processes reserved for CPU-bound tasks.
That moved the bottleneck off the CPU and onto the task queue.
Defined a staged path to a Go-based control plane for the next performance ceiling.
items.outcome: Fleet capacity went from 8–10 to 100 concurrent robots on the same 4-core / 16 GB hardware.

items.title: Billing platform at scale
items.summary: An app serving 900K+ bill views a day, with much smaller bundles.
items.problem: At Razorpay I worked on billing and CRM product surfaces that served a lot of traffic.
approach: Worked on an app serving 900K+ bill views a day, and dashboards for digital billing and CRM with Node.js, Express and Kubernetes.
A React 18 migration made frontend bundles 90% smaller.
Migrated a legacy site to Razorpay PG with a microfrontend architecture.
items.outcome: The app served 900K+ bill views a day, and its frontend bundles became 90% smaller.
